question: Should I sign the lease on the Route 1 storefront for our second location now?
leaning: Sign it. The board told us to test first; we ran the 90-day test, and the conditions it set are now met.

profile.name: Rise & Shine Bakery
profile.size: 1 location, 10 employees, including a full-time manager
profile.budget: $108,000 in savings, plus a $35,000 SBA microloan approved for equipment
goals: don't put the first store at risk
profile.constraints: 90-day test results. First store: netted $6,100, $5,800 and $6,400 a month after my $5,000 salary, reconciled by my bookkeeper; revenue is now $47,000 a month, and last summer's 20% dip still broke even. Square Online delivery: $4,300 a month at $3.90 profit per order after fees; DoorDash lost money, so I stopped it at day 60. Staff: my manager and a second employee both hold the certified food service manager credential; the manager has run the first store without me for ten weeks and will keep it. Route 1 demand: six Saturday pop-ups in the space averaged $1,150, 70% from customers new to our Square directory. Space: a former cafe 1.5 miles away with a hood, grease trap and three-phase power. Lease, reviewed by my attorney: $2,950 a month gross, 3% yearly increases, three years plus a renewal option, bakery exclusive, no personal guarantee, and an exit after 12 months for four months' rent. A signed letter from the landlord pays the $40,000 allowance to the contractor in two draws, covers any hood, grease trap or electrical repairs, and starts rent at the occupancy permit, followed by three months free. Build-out: a fixed-price $52,000 contract, so our share is $12,000 plus a $5,200 contingency. The SBA lender confirmed in writing that the $35,000 microloan pays for equipment at signing. Prince George's County health plan review for a former food space takes 6-8 weeks, per our pre-application meeting. Cash: about $23,000 comes out of savings, leaving $85,000. Downside case built with the Maryland SBDC (Route 1 at 60% of the first store's sales, a 30% overrun, a two-month late opening, a summer dip): the first store stays profitable and savings never fall below $78,000. The landlord needs an answer within two weeks.
